nameStory: Boreal yarrow gets its name from its northern home - 'boreal' refers to the northern forest regions of Canada and Alaska. Like its more common cousin, it shares the yarrow name, which comes from the legendary Greek hero Achilles, who supposedly used yarrow plants to heal his soldiers' wounds on the battlefield.
description: Boreal yarrow is a rare northern wildflower that looks very similar to common yarrow but calls the far north home. It grows as a sturdy perennial herb reaching about 1-3 feet tall, with feathery, fern-like leaves and clusters of small white flowers arranged in flat-topped groups. This hardy plant is built for cold climates and harsh conditions, making it an extremely uncommon find in New England. When you do spot it, you'll notice it has that distinctive yarrow look - delicate flowers atop strong stems with soft, divided leaves.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Soft, feathery leaves that are deeply divided into tiny segments, giving them a lace-like or fern-like appearance. Run your fingers along them - they feel almost silky and have a strong, somewhat medicinal smell when crushed.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white flowers (sometimes with a hint of pink) clustered together in flat-topped groups about 2-4 inches across. Each 'flower' is actually many small flowers packed together, typical of the daisy family.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows in sturdy clumps from underground stems, typically 1-3 feet tall with straight, unbranched stems until the flower cluster at the top.

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Strong, upright stems that feel firm and slightly fuzzy to the touch, often with a reddish tinge, especially toward the base.

habitat: In New England, boreal yarrow would most likely be found in cold, rocky areas at higher elevations - think mountain slopes, rocky meadows, or disturbed soils in cooler microclimates. It prefers well-drained soils and can tolerate poor, rocky conditions where other plants struggle. Given its extreme rarity here (only one recorded observation), it's probably a chance visitor from much further north or an isolated population in a particularly cold, harsh spot.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as small rosettes of feathery leaves close to the ground. The distinctive fern-like foliage is the main identifying feature during this season.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time with flat-topped clusters of small white flowers appearing from June through August. This is when the plant is most noticeable and easiest to identify.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and develop into small, dry seeds. Leaves may begin to yellow but often stay somewhat green longer than many other plants.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to underground parts in our climate, leaving little trace above ground except possibly some dried stems in protected spots.

funFact: Boreal yarrow is so rare in New England that it's been spotted here only once! This plant is essentially a 'lost tourist' from the far north - it's much more at home in places like northern Canada and Alaska, where it thrives in conditions that would freeze out most of our familiar wildflowers.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with common yarrow, which is abundant throughout New England. The key difference is location - if you find yarrow in a typical New England field, roadside, or garden, it's almost certainly common yarrow. Boreal yarrow would only be in very cold, harsh, high-elevation spots and is incredibly rare here.
contextualKnowledge: Don't expect to find this plant on your typical nature walk! With only one recorded observation in all of New England, boreal yarrow is more of a botanical curiosity than a regular wildflower here. Most 'yarrow' you'll encounter will be the common species, which looks very similar but is perfectly happy in our warmer climate.
compareHints: Boreal yarrow is nearly identical to common yarrow in appearance - both have the same feathery leaves and white flower clusters. The main differences are habitat preferences and hardiness: boreal yarrow needs much colder conditions and is adapted for harsh northern climates, while common yarrow thrives in temperate areas and disturbed soils. If you're seeing yarrow in a typical New England setting, it's almost certainly the common species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common yarrow differs from sneezewort (its closest New England relative) by having finely divided, feathery leaves instead of simple, lance-shaped leaves.
Unlike its relative common yarrow with deeply divided, feathery leaves, sneezewort has simple, narrow leaves with toothed edges.
Fern-leaf yarrow stands out from its relatives by being the tallest yarrow species and having the most intensely golden-yellow flowers.
